objective: Deep-dive technical investigation and interactive ablation simulator of Dynamic Reasoning Compute Budgets, demonstrating how test-time scaling, thinking tokens, and self-correction backtracking transform reasoning performance.
audience: AI researchers, machine learning engineers, and system architects

claims: Inference-time compute scaling can surpass models with 14x more pre-training parameters on hard reasoning tasks
Test-time compute spans three distinct operational regimes: Sequential CoT, Leaf-level Best-of-N, and Prefix-level Tree Search
Autonomous backtracking emerges naturally under binary verifiable rewards as models learn to detect and discard flawed hypotheses
Layer-wise token revision differentiates genuine deep-thinking tokens from superficial conversational padding
Frontier 2026 models deploy adaptive thinking budgets ranging from 0 to 256,000 tokens based on prompt difficulty
functions: Interactive Dynamic Reasoning Compute Ablation Lab
Search Strategy Selector (Sequential CoT vs Best-of-N vs Tree Search)
Dynamic Token Budget Slider (256 to 64,000 tokens)
Task Complexity Tier Selector (Easy to Frontier Repo Bug)
Interactive Trace Visualizer illustrating backtracking and branch pruning
observable_effects: Increasing token budget on hard problems dramatically improves pass rate, while producing diminishing returns and wasted cost on elementary tasks
Switching between Sequential CoT and Best-of-N demonstrates the trade-off between single-thread latency and parallel GPU sample costs
Toggling task difficulty activates different optimal search regimes according to Snell et al. scaling laws

rules: Ground all test-time compute equations in published academic literature
Differentiate empirical benchmarks from interactive browser simulation models
Detail failure modes including token inflation, latency overhead, and verifier score dilution
